read.sections.0.heading.source: AI needs a lot of human work
read.sections.0.heading.back: AI needs a lot of human work

read.sections.0.text.source: AI tools seem to work by themselves, but many people help to make them. For some kinds of training, people add a label to each example. A worker might tag thousands of photos as “bus”, “tree” or “person”. Other workers rate a tool's answers, to test and improve it. Moderators check harmful posts, so a tool learns what it must not show. Many tools also learned from words and pictures on the internet. Some writers and artists say nobody asked them first. In the made-up Ask Me tool, Amara adds labels, Tomas is a moderator, and Lin's stories are in the data.
read.sections.0.text.back: AI tools look like they work by themselves, but many people help make them. For some kinds of training, people add a label to each example. A worker might mark thousands of photos as “bus”, “tree” or “person”. Other workers rate a tool's answers, to test and improve it. Moderators check harmful posts, so that the tool learns what it must not show. Many tools also learned from words and pictures on the internet. Some writers and artists say that nobody asked their permission first. In the made-up Ask Me tool, Amara adds labels, Tomas is a moderator, and Lin's stories are in its data.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: Many people help make AI tools. For some training, people add labels to examples. A worker may mark many photos “bus” or “tree”. Other workers check whether answers are good. Moderators check posts that could hurt people. Many tools also learned from words and pictures on the internet. Some writers and artists say nobody asked their permission.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Some of this work is far away and low paid
read.sections.1.heading.back: Some of this work is far away and its pay is low

read.sections.1.text.source: Much of this work is done online in countries such as Kenya and the Philippines, often for companies in richer countries. In January 2023, a news magazine reported on about three dozen workers in Kenya. In 2021 and 2022, they labelled harmful text for a well-known AI tool's safety filter. They took home about 1.32 to 2 US dollars an hour. The AI company paid the company in the middle 12.50 dollars an hour for their work, which that company said also paid other costs. In August 2023, a newspaper spoke to 36 online workers in the Philippines. All but two said some of their wages came late, were cut or never came. Their platform said this was rare.
read.sections.1.text.back: Much of this work is done online in countries like Kenya and the Philippines, often for companies in richer countries. In January 2023, a news magazine reported on about three dozen workers in Kenya. In 2021 and 2022, they labelled harmful text for the safety filter of a well-known AI tool. They took home about 1.32 to 2 US dollars per hour. That AI company paid the go-between company 12.50 dollars per hour for their work, and the go-between company said that money was also used for other costs. In August 2023, a newspaper spoke with 36 online workers in the Philippines. All except two said some of their wages were late, cut or never paid. Their platform said this rarely happens.
read.sections.1.text.note: "About three dozen" as "sekitar tiga puluhan" (about thirty-some). "The company in the middle" as "perusahaan perantara" (go-between company). Decimal commas (1,32; 12,50), as Indonesian writes them.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Much of this work is done online, in Kenya, the Philippines and other places. Often, the firms that pay are in richer countries. In 2023, a magazine wrote about Kenyan workers. They labelled harmful text for an AI tool. They got less than 2 US dollars an hour. The AI firm paid 12.50 dollars an hour to a firm in the middle. That firm said the money also paid other costs. In the Philippines, a newspaper spoke to 36 workers. Nearly all said some wages were late, cut or missing. The firm said this was rare.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Much of this work is done online, in Kenya, the Philippines and other places. Often, the companies that pay are in richer countries. In 2023, a magazine wrote about workers in Kenya. They labelled harmful text for an AI tool. They got less than 2 US dollars per hour. That AI company paid 12.50 dollars per hour to a go-between company. That company said the money was also used for other costs. In the Philippines, a newspaper spoke with 36 workers. Almost all said some of their wages were late, cut or missing. The company said this rarely happens.

read.sections.2.heading.source: An old question about fair work
read.sections.2.heading.back: An old question about fair work

read.sections.2.text.source: Unfair work is not new. In the 1800s, people in England began to call very low-paid, hard work “sweating”, and later spoke of a sweatshop. Today, some people call online labelling a “digital sweatshop”. Like clothes, AI has a long supply chain, and users rarely see the people behind it. In July 2023, Oxford researchers rated 15 online work platforms, some of them selling AI data work. They checked pay, conditions, contracts, management and a voice for workers. None met their basic standards; the best scored 5 out of 10. But platforms differ: some changed their rules after the researchers asked, for example by setting a minimum wage.
read.sections.2.text.back: Unfair work is not new. In the 1800s, people in England began to call hard work with very low pay “sweating”, and later the word sweatshop appeared. Now, some people call online labelling work a “digital sweatshop”. Like clothes, AI has a long supply chain, and users rarely see the people behind it. In July 2023, researchers in Oxford rated 15 online work platforms, some of which sell data work for AI. They checked pay, working conditions, contracts, management and a voice for workers. None met their basic standards; the best score was 5 out of 10. But the platforms were different: some changed their rules after the researchers asked, for example by setting a minimum wage.
read.sections.2.text.note: "Sweatshop" is kept in English (the key word), as Indonesian news writing does, with "sweating" glossed as "berkeringat" so the history of the word makes sense; the glossary explains it. "Supply chain" as "rantai pasok", the term Indonesian government and business writing uses.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Unfair work is not new. In the 1800s, people in England called very low-paid work “sweating”. Later came the word “sweatshop”. None met all the basic rules. But they were not all the same. Some changed their rules after the study.

watch.summary.source: In this news interview, a reporter talks with an expert. The expert works for a group that wants AI to be used in a fair way. She explains that AI tools need lots of data. A computer does not know by itself if a picture shows a cat or a dog. People must look at the pictures and label them, again and again. Then the tool can learn. A lot of this work is done online, in poorer parts of the world, because the pay there is lower. Some workers must look at harmful posts, so other people don't have to see them. The pay is often very low. Workers are not always sure they will be paid. The expert says AI is really built on human work and human thinking. She hopes for clear rules to protect these workers.
watch.summary.back: In this news interview, a reporter speaks with an expert. That expert works at a group that wants AI to be used in a fair way. She explains that AI tools need lots of data. A computer does not know by itself whether a picture shows a cat or a dog. People must look at those pictures and label them, again and again. Then the tool can learn. Much of this work is done online, in poorer parts of the world, because the pay there is lower. Some workers must look at harmful posts, so that other people don't need to see them. The pay is often very low. Workers are not always sure that they will be paid. The expert says that AI is really built on human work and human thinking. She hopes there will be clear rules to protect these workers.

sensitiveNotes.1.source: Work and money: many learners can't work legally, and people close to them may do low-paid, informal or online work. Never ask about learners' or their families' jobs, pay or money. Keep the discussion on the made-up Ask Me workers and the reported facts. Words like “sweatshop” and “unfair pay” may feel close to home; let learners speak if they want to, without pressing.
sensitiveNotes.1.back: Work and money: many learners are not allowed to work officially by law, and people close to them may do low-paid, informal or online work. Never ask about the jobs, pay or money of learners or their families. Keep the discussion on the made-up Ask Me workers and the reported facts. Words like “sweatshop” and “unfair pay” may feel close to their lives; let learners speak if they want to, without pressing.

educatorNotes.0.source: The facts are dated and their scope matters. TIME (18 January 2023): about three dozen workers at an outsourcing firm in Kenya labelled harmful text for a safety filter from November 2021 to early 2022 and took home about $1.32 to $2 an hour; the AI company's contract paid the firm $12.50 an hour. The firm said that rate covered all its costs (offices, managers, benefits) and that workers earned $1.46 to $3.74 an hour after tax. The Washington Post (28 August 2023): 34 of 36 freelance workers in the Philippines said payments had been delayed, reduced or cancelled; the platform said delays were “exceedingly rare” and that it pays a living wage. Fairwork's Cloudwork Ratings (Oxford Internet Institute, July 2023) scored 15 online work platforms, not all of them AI work, on fair pay, conditions, contracts, management and representation: scores ran from 0 to 5 out of 10, none met its minimum standards, and four platforms made 17 changes after Fairwork's suggestions (two adopted minimum-wage policies). These reports describe particular workers, firms and platforms, not every AI job. The companies (OpenAI, Sama, Scale AI and its Remotasks platform) are named only in sources and here, as the Digital World spec asks. Writers' and artists' work: in 2023 some writers and artists sued AI companies or asked for consent, credit and pay. Companies did not all take one position: some argued that training on public material is lawful (fair use in the US), some declined to comment, and one news agency licensed its archive to an AI company (Anchorage Daily News, from The Washington Post, July 2023). Court cases have moved on since; check the latest before teaching that part, and don't tell learners that all creative work was taken without asking. The claim record is in content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW05.md.
